articles.title: 92nd annual meeting of Indian Academy of Sciences to begin at NCESS on November 13
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The meeting brings together eminent scientists, researchers and academicians from across India

The 92nd Annual Meeting of the Indian Academy of Sciences (IASc), hosted by the National Centre for Earth Science Studies (NCESS), Thiruvananthapuram, will be held on Friday and Saturday. The meeting brings together eminent scientists, researchers and academicians from across India.
At a press conference here on Thursday, senior scientists underscored the importance of strengthening scientific research and education.

Raghavan Varadarajan, president, IASc; N.V. Chalapathi Rao, director, NCESS; Hemalatha Balaram, chairperson, Science Academies’ Education Panel, IASc; K.K. Ramachandran, ex-officio Principal Secretary, Science and Technology department, Government of Keralam, and executive vice-president, KSCSTE; and Tomson J. Kallukalam, Scientist-F and group head, Solid Earth Research Group, NCESS, addressed the press conference.

As part of the programme, the Science Academies’ Education Panel (SEP) Symposium for Teachers, titled ‘Frontiers in Science,’ was conducted on Thursday. The symposium was aimed at connecting teachers with current scientific research and emerging developments across disciplines.

articles.title: Military helicopter crashes in southern Turkey, killing 4
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The aircraft crashed for unknown reasons in Samankoy, a neighbourhood on the southern outskirts of the provincial capital Malatya in the evening
A military helicopter crashed in southern Turkiye on Thursday (November 12, 2026), killing four personnel, the Turkish Defence Ministry said.
The aircraft crashed for unknown reasons in Samankoy, a neighbourhood on the southern outskirts of the provincial capital Malatya in the evening.

“As a result of an accident involving our S-70 helicopter in Malatya, for a reason not yet determined, 4 of our heroic comrades-in-arms aboard the helicopter were martyred,” the Ministry said in a social media post. “We pray that God will have mercy on our martyrs and offer our condolences and prayers for strength to their grieving families, our Turkish Armed Forces, and our noble nation.”

TV images showed the wreckage of the helicopter burning near a cluster of buildings in an otherwise open area of land. The Demiroren News Agency reported that flames had spread to a nearby house but reported no casualties on the ground.
Police, firefighters and medical teams were dispatched to the crash.
The Sikorsky S-70 is widely used as a transport helicopter by militaries across the world. Its variants include the Black Hawk, which can carry up to 11 soldiers plus its air crew.
The Turkish Air Force operates a large base — the 7th Main Jet Base — to the north of Malatya.

articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: As AI infrastructure expands, residents question its impact on everyday life amid growing demands on local resources and public utilities

“Hey, what do you think of the data centre that’s coming up right across the street from here? I see a lot of construction happening around us all the time,” I ask my colleague Kevin, sounding innocent and naïve, for my Swedish friends had warned me — when I was moving to the U.S. earlier this year — not to touch politics or any sensitive topic at the workplace in America. Instead, talk about family, they had recommended. I didn’t know where data centres fell on that spectrum.

Kevin stiffens. We are having lunch. He carefully places his fork down and looks past me through the window, where a dusty haze from the construction is floating in the hot Texan air, and starts talking softly.

“You know, no one in Dallas wants this! This data centre will run us dry and take all the residents’ water. Water pressure at home has already dropped, and it’ll make our electricity bills higher,” says Kevin, and then looks straight into my eyes and asks, “Why are we paying for this? Anyone vote on this?”
I didn’t have any answers and decide to gently steer the conversation in a different direction. But the question remains alive inside me.
Aerial view of a portion of the Meta Prometheus Campus, an AI data centre and supercluster project, in New Albany, Ohio. | Photo Credit: Getty Images

Until recently, data centres primarily served the needs of cloud computing, search, streaming and e-commerce. However, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed the equation because training and operating large AI models require vast amounts of specialised computing power that these newly constructed data centres aim to provide.

AI models, especially generative ones such as Claude and ChatGPT, need huge amounts of processing power and data storage to be trained and used. They come from massive data centres that house special chips, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), to handle these demanding AI tasks quickly.

According to Cushman & Wakefield, a global real estate services firm, the U.S. is by far the most dominant data centre market in the world, and there are, at this point, more than 1,500 data centre projects underway across the country. Within the U.S., the state of Virginia alone has more than 11 GW (gigawatt) of operational data centre capability in 2026, and Dallas is catching up fast.

India is witnessing a similar expansion. According to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, the country’s installed data-centre capacity has grown from around 375 MW in 2020 to approximately 1,575 MW today. The Central Electricity Authority estimates that power demand from data centres could reach nearly 17 GW by 2031-32. Google, meanwhile, is investing $15 billion over five years in an AI hub in Visakhapatnam, including a data-centre campus with an initial capacity of 1 GW. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian has called it the company’s largest AI hub outside the U.S., saying that the company’s “long-term vision” is to accelerate India’s own AI mission.
A view Inside the NTT data centre campus in Garland, Texas, March 2026. | Photo Credit: Getty Images

optsEn: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
optsHi: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
optsMr: Critical ban: On recycling of lithium-ion batteries
dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: India needs to create an entire ecosystem for recycling of lithium-ion batteries

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: On November 10, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass by moving it from the “free” to the “prohibited” list of exports. Black mass is an intermediate product when spent batteries and factory scrap are shredded. It contains valuable lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. The Commerce Ministry says the ban will ensure feedstock for domestic refiners, lift their capacity utilisation and draw investment. While the recycling of lead-acid batteries end-to-end is an established ecosystem and formalised, too, lithium-ion battery recycling is an emerging segment with only a few dozen licensed operators but has much potential given the scale of use of such batteries in EVs. While the ban will redirect supply, it will not automatically create a market and ecosystem. Just banning export without creating an entire ecosystem will only lead to dumping of lithium-ion batteries into landfills if the blackmass has no market. Blackmass production is a largely mechanical process but further downstream processing is more specialised chemical processing requiring larger investment and further policy support. If downstream units are online, their output can directly feed into indigenous lithium-ion battery manufacture.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: critical minerals / minerals / exports / economy, business and finance / business (general)

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: India must improve ties with Bangladesh, and protect Hasina

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Bangladesh’s former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina now in exile in India, has set off speculation about her imminent return to Dhaka by submitting an application for a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card this week. The application, made through the Bangladesh High Commission in Delhi, was dismissed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir, who said that the government in Dhaka would not grant a passport to a “terrorist”, and would seek her return via the extradition agreement as a “prisoner transfer process” with India. Ms. Hasina has already announced that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December this year, as she did after her previous stay in India in exile from 1975-1981, after the brutal assassination of her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and nearly every other member of her family. However, the situation is considerably different now. This time, Ms. Hasina came to India in 2024 fleeing mobs of protestors that overthrew her government, and has since been convicted by a tribunal for ordering a crackdown on thousands of students, and sentenced to death. In interviews, including to The Hindu , Ms. Hasina says she hopes to return to Bangladesh to argue her case and rebuild her party, the Awami League, but that is hardly likely, given the anger against her amongst the polity, and bipartisan consensus to ban the Awami League from politics. Despite the harsh rhetoric it employs against her, the BNP government is unlikely to wish for her return, as it would have to begin execution proceedings against the 79-year-old former Prime Minister, with international opposition to such a move expected to be voluble. Not doing so would only strengthen its opposition party, the Jamaat-e-Islami, that has accused the Rahman government of soft-pedalling the issue. The government must also worry about possible protests and violence within the country in the event Ms. Hasina returns.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Editorial Context: In a dilemma: On Sheikh Hasina and India-Bangladesh ties. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Nations must deliver on past promises before committing to lofty climate goals

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The 31st Conference of Parties (COP) began this week in Antalya, Türkiye. Hosted by Türkiye and negotiations presided over by Australia, the run-up to the gathering saw ministerial delegations visit Fiji and Tuvalu. This was to serve as a stark reminder of the purpose of COPs, namely that it was small island nations that are most vulnerable to warming from rising greenhouse gas emissions. However, the opening days have belied this sense of urgency. Prominent world leaders, even from the European countries who as a group champion the cause most vociferously, have chosen to skip the meet. The agenda and pre-summit expectations suggest that the main concerns this year are likely to be about delivering on existing commitments such as delivering $300 billion a year by 2035, which was decided at COP29 in Baku, as well as the COP30 call to triple the adaptation finance during that interval. However, deciding how these climate funds will practically flow has been deferred to COP32. The second global stocktake, a periodic check on progress under the Paris Agreement, begins at COP31, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has dithered on a timeline for the next reports that will serve as the scientific push to policy makers to accelerate efforts towards keeping a rise in temperatures below 2°C, and more ambitiously 1.5°C.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: This year’s Booker Prize betrays an anxiety about AI’s place in society

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: A defining feature of the world today is that knowledge is proliferating and societies are struggling to agree on what is happening. AI models have significantly catalysed this devolution, allowing bad actors to flood spaces ranging from the research literature to public airwaves with questionable information, and drawing the attention of governments worldwide to the security implications of such a potent technology. The Booker Prize for M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything , a novel about a sense-defying alien invasion and the unsettling prospect of un-understandability it confronts humans with, effectively acknowledges the centrality of the AI question both through the book’s substance and the judges’ choice. A consequence of rampant AI use has been an assault on people’s attention span as well as the ability to make sense of new claims, so much so that reliable, verifiable meaning has become a premium entity. The novel, on the other hand, attempts to diagnose a post-meaning world in which people are only left to look inward. The Prize is also a long-overdue victory for the merits of science fiction, a genre that Harrison helped shape from the late 1960s, and one that English literature’s top honours have repeatedly overlooked. That said, the novel itself is far from being its best example, including because Harrison’s diagnosis lets technology and the practice of power off the hook for their failures.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: award-winning books / books and publishing / Artificial Intelligence

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: The overturning of the mandate in the Gokul Dairy cooperative is disturbing

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Amid a nationwide outcry over electoral malpractices, with fresh evidence emerging every day, the BJP government in Maharashtra has gone a step further in overturning a popular mandate through an executive fiat. It approved changing the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act through an ordinance on November 4 — which the Governor promulgated on November 6 — with the immediate effect of facilitating the takeover of the Kolhapur District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union, popularly known as Gokul Dairy , by the BJP and its allies. A Congress-led panel won 13 of the 25 elected seats on the board of the cooperative on October 19. Gokul, which is one of Maharashtra’s most influential cooperative institutions, has an annual turnover of around ₹4,000 crore and is linked to several lakh milk producers in western Maharashtra. The BJP had set its eyes on the cooperative sector as yet another arena of its political dominance, creating a Ministry of Cooperation under Home Minister Amit Shah. While that plan of controlling cooperatives continues to play out through various means, the overturning of an election clearly won by the Congress-led Opposition marks a new level of brazenness by the BJP, and of the impunity its actions continue to receive from the judiciary.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Maharashtra / Bharatiya Janata Party / government / Indian National Congress / politics

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Exclusion of creamy layer is essential, but must be done consistently

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: If public resources are to dismantle both caste hierarchy and class inequality, OBC reservation should resist the notion that caste disadvantage makes economic differences among OBC families irrelevant. The ‘creamy layer’ rules are responsible for identifying those OBC members who have advanced sufficiently to no longer require affirmative action. However, the government has implemented them inconsistently. The Supreme Court in March corrected one inconsistency, that the government cannot hold the salary alone of an OBC candidate’s parent as evidence of social advancement. In Indra Sawhney (1992) , the Court upheld the government’s 27% reservation for OBC candidates in central government services if it also excluded economically advanced sections, i.e., the creamy layer, among OBCs. Following the equivalence requirement issued in 1993, the Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) issued a “clarification” in 2004 that the government used, from around 2015, to deny dozens of OBC candidates who had cleared the Civil Services Examination their benefits because their parents’ salaries exceeded the official threshold due to pay revisions that did not always reflect changes in occupational status. The Cabinet also approved equivalence guidelines in 2017 but a parliamentary committee criticised it over a number of issues.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: Reservation / court / Caste / labour / government / Census 2027
